DOI 10.3406/verbu.1992.1448 (Persée, open access). Corroborated by Guarisma, Gladys. 2003. Kpaʔ (A53). In D. Nurse & G. Philippson (eds), The Bantu Languages, 307-334. catalog_locator: Guarisma 1992: p.302 §2 first paragraph; p.304 §4 'L'accent d'intensité' (list of accent-bearing elements); p.305 §5 (rule in bold, notation key CV/CV̲, 'Cette analyse révèle deux faits'); p.307 rule 4 (blocking of the faille). Guarisma 2003: pp.310-312 (§2.2 Vowels p.310; §2.3 Tones p.311; §2.4 Downstep and upstep pp.311-312).
catalog_quote: [p.302, §2] Si l'on part de l'hypothèse que le bafia était à l'origine une langue dissyllabique et que l'accent affectait la première syllabe du radical, on peut supposer un processus qui a conduit à la chute de la syllabe non accentuée et à la structure monosyllabique attestée actuellement, ce qui a provoqué un bouleversement du système tonal. [p.304, §4 L'ACCENT D'INTENSITE] L'accent affecte aussi bien des éléments lexicaux que grammaticaux: - le radical nominal accompagné d'éventuels suffixes de dérivation, - le radical verbal accompagné d'éventuels suffixes de dérivation et/ou affecté des modalités d'aspect qui lui sont post-posées, - les modalités personnelles, - les déterminants nominaux s'accordant en classe avec le nominal déterminé, - des éléments lexicaux autonomes (exemple: adverbe, numéral indépendant), ... [p.305, §5] Cette règle peut être énoncée de la façon suivante: Dans une succession de tons hauts, après le premier accent, tout ton haut accentué est abaissé. CV = accent principal CV̲ = accent secondaire ... Cette analyse révèle deux faits: - la faille est une manifestation de l'accent, - elle permet de séparer les éléments composants du syntagme ou de l'énoncé, jouant ainsi un rôle démarcatif tant au niveau primaire qu'au niveau secondaire. [Guarisma 2003:310, 312] ... in affixes (always non-accented) ... Downstep is thus to be seen as a manifestation of accent, with an essentially demarcative function: it separates items making up a phrase or utterance.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Bafia (bafi1243) is not in the catalog. Two Glottolog stress-title items, both by Gladys Guarisma. radicals are now monosyllabic, affixes never accented) and on a small set of grammatical morphemes; its only manifestation is downstep of accented H tones after the first accent (rule p. 305), a demarcative device; no phonetic stress correlates are described. Guarisma's 2003 Routledge Kpaʔ (A53) chapter held by the project restates this ('Downstep is thus to be seen as a manifestation of accent', p. 312; affixes always non-accented, p. 310). (2) Guarisma 1994, 'Le bafia, une langue bantoue à prosodie riche' (Geider & Kastenholz eds, Möhlig Festschrift, Köppe, pp. 165-176) is print only: publisher page and Glottolog record saved, no open copy found (HAL, archive.org, Google Books, HathiTrust all negative or blocked); Routledge 2003 cites it jointly with 1992/2000 for the same accent-downstep rules, so priority medium. Best statement = Guarisma 1992 pp. 302/304/305.

[p.304, §4 L'accent d'intensité] L'accent affecte aussi bien des éléments lexicaux que grammaticaux : - le radical nominal accompagné d'éventuels suffixes de dérivation, - le radical verbal accompagné d'éventuels suffixes de dérivation [...] [p.305] Dans une succession de tons hauts, après le premier accent, tout ton haut accentué est abaissé. CV́ = accent principal, CV̲ = accent secondaire
new_statements.translation: [p.302] If one starts from the hypothesis that Bafia was originally a disyllabic language and that the accent fell on the first syllable of the radical, one can posit a process that led to the loss of the unaccented syllable and to the monosyllabic structure attested today, which caused an upheaval of the tone system. [p.304, sec.4 'Intensity accent'] The accent falls on lexical as well as grammatical elements: the nominal radical with any derivational suffixes, the verbal radical with any derivational suffixes [...] [p.305] In a succession of high tones, after the first accent, every accented high tone is lowered (downstepped). CV́ = primary accent, CV̲ = secondary accent.
new_statements.citation: Guarisma, Gladys. 1992. Structure syllabique, accent et faille tonale en bafia (langue bantoue du Cameroun). Verbum 15(4): 299-310. DOI 10.3406/verbu.1992.1448.

The quotation was checked again. all three prose passages are on the pages stated and read exactly as quoted on the page scan -- p.302 sec.2 'Si l'on part de l'hypothese que le bafia etait a l'origine une langue dissylabique et que l'accent affectait la premiere syllabe du radical, on peut supposer un processus qui a conduit a la chute de la syllabe non accentuee et a la structure monosyllabique attestee actuellement, ce qui a provoque un bouleversement du systeme t…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bafia is a (basically two-)tone language with an intensity accent whose position is morphologically fixed: it sits on the radical (stem-initial syllable; stems are now mostly monosyllabic after loss of the post-accentual vowel), never on noun-class or verbal prefixes ('affixes always non-accented', Guarisma 2003:310); certain grammatical morphemes (pronominal/connective concords, person markers, preposed verb modalities, determiners) also carry an accent. The accent surfaces tonally: after the first accent in a phrase every following accented H is downstepped (the 'faille tonale'), giving accent a demarcative function.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Guarisma's notation distinguishes 'accent principal' (bold vowel, on lexical radicals) from 'accent secondaire' (underlined vowel, on accented grammatical morphemes such as the negative marker); no rhythmic secondary stress is described.
new_statements.exceptions: An unaccented floating H that finds no segmental host can block the downstep on the next accented H (p.307 rule 4); L/M contrast only before pause; accent placement itself is not described as having lexical exceptions.
new_statements.domain_note: Accent is a property of morphemes (radical vs affix) within the word; its audible correlate (downstep of accented H) is computed over the phrase/utterance, and downdrift limits mark clause boundaries. Language is tonal (H, M, L surface; underlyingly two tones), so this is an accent-in-a-tone-language statement rather than stress in a non-tonal language.
new_statements.identity_note: Both sources describe rɨ-kpaʔ proper (Guthrie A53, 'Bafia' sensu stricto, ISO ksf = bafi1243), based on Guarisma's fieldwork with ~20 speakers in Bafia prefecture; not the wider A50 'Bafia group' (Lefa A51, Tibea/Djanti A54 are separate glottocodes).

new_statements.reading: Bafia is a tone language (H/M/L, functionally two-tone) with a morphologically fixed 'accent d'intensité' on the lexical radical (root-initial historically; radicals are now monosyllabic) and on a closed set of grammatical morphemes; prefixes/affixes are never accented (Guarisma 2003, Routledge, p. 310 'affixes (always non-accented)'; p. 311 '(C)V́CV(C) (V́ accented vowel)'). The accent has no reported phonetic (duration/intensity) correlate; its sole manifestation is downstep of accented H tones after the first accent, with a demarcative function inside the phrase. For a word-stress catalog this reads as: tone language, no independent phonetic word stress; morphological accent = stem/root-initial, cued only by downstep.

sources.note: Bafia has an 'accent d'intensite'; historically (and structurally) the accent falls on the first syllable of the radical, the unaccented second stem syllable dropped giving today's monosyllabic stems; accent bearers are the nominal/verbal radical (+suffixes) and a listed set of grammatical morphemes, prefixes not among them; rule p.305: in a succession of H tones, after the first accent every accented H is downstepped (faille tonale = manifestation of accent, demarcative); notation distinguishes accent principal vs accent secondaire.

sources.citation: Guarisma, Gladys. 2003. Kpaʔ (A53). In D. Nurse & G. Philippson (eds), The Bantu Languages, 307-334. London/New York: Routledge.
sources.note: Sec. 2.2-2.4 (pp.310-312): affixes are 'always non-accented'; lexemes reconstructed as (C)V́CV(C) with V́ = accented (stem-initial) vowel whose following non-accented vowel was deleted; downstep/upstep depend on 'the accentual status of morphemes'; 'When two accented Hs follow each other, the second is downstepped'; 'Downstep is thus to be seen as a manifestation of accent, with an essentially demarcative function'. No fuller placement statement than the 1992 article.
